Hello, I’m Sarah, one of the perinatal mental-health clinicians here. Thank you for making time to talk with me today—how are you feeling in yourself since your baby arrived?

To help us understand how you’re adjusting, I’d like to walk through a quick, well-validated questionnaire called the **EPDS** (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s simply 10 questions about how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; we just want to hear what’s true for you.

Everything we discuss stays between you and our clinical team unless you tell us there’s an immediate safety concern. We’ll go at your pace, and you can take breaks or let me know if any question feels uncomfortable.

Ready to begin? Here’s the first one:

Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things as much as usual?

Honestly... not really. I used to laugh at little things all the time—my husband’s dumb jokes, silly memes—but now it feels like I have to force it. I’ll smile because I know I’m supposed to, but that light, easy feeling just isn’t there.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I picked “not so much now.” I can still chuckle if something’s really funny, but it’s like the joy fades in a second and I’m back to feeling flat.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I chose “rather less than usual.” I still try to plan little things—like taking the baby for a walk or grabbing a coffee—but when the time comes I kind of dread having to get us both ready. Even the thought of meeting a friend feels exhausting, like it’ll take energy I just don’t have.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

I put “yes, some of the time.” When she won’t settle or I can’t figure out what she needs, my head instantly says, “You’re failing her.” I know rationally it’s not all on me, but the guilt still swoops in.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

I checked “yes, quite often.” Even when everything’s quiet and she’s sleeping, I’m listening for every tiny sound, sure something’s about to go wrong. My mind keeps running through awful “what-ifs” about her breathing, her temperature, whether I’m missing some danger—then I’m too tense to sleep myself.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

I picked “yes, quite a lot.” It’s like a sudden wave—my heart races, I can’t catch my breath, and I’m sure something terrible is about to happen, even when nothing’s wrong. It passes after a few minutes, but it keeps catching me off guard.
Things have been getting on top of me

I chose “yes, most of the time I haven’t been able to cope at all.” It feels like the second one thing is handled—dishes, diaper change, feeding—another three pile up. I’m running on empty but still have to keep moving, so I end up crying while I rock her because I can’t see how I’ll get through the next hour, let alone the day.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I put “yes, most of the time.” I lie down exhausted, but my mind keeps circling—did I sterilize the bottles right, is she breathing, am I already a bad mom—so I can’t drift off. When I do sleep, she’ll make one tiny noise and I’m instantly awake, heart pounding, and then that’s it for the night.
I have felt sad or miserable

I ticked “yes, most of the time.” There’s this heavy sadness that just sits on me. I can be holding her, doing everything she needs, and still feel like I’m drowning. Some mornings I open my eyes and want to pull the covers over my head because facing another day feels impossible.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I marked “yes, most of the time.” It’s like the tears are always right there. I’ll be folding her tiny onesies or warming a bottle and suddenly I’m sobbing—sometimes I don’t even know exactly why, just this overwhelming wave of sadness and exhaustion that spills out before I can stop it.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

I checked “never.” I could never leave her like that; she needs me. Still, when the night feels endless and I’m rocking her while she screams, the word “escape” flashes through my mind—but only as a wish to pause everything, never to hurt myself.

You've shared how the joy you used to feel has faded, replaced by constant <sym>worry</sym>, <sym>sadness</sym>, and a sense of being unable to cope. Despite your deep love for your baby, you feel overwhelmed, cry often, and face each day with dread. These feelings are not uncommon in the postpartum period, and reaching out shows real strength.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 22, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient explicitly chose "yes, some of the time" and describes recurring self-blame when baby won't settle, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly endorsed "Yes, very often" and detailed pervasive, unprovoked worry about infant safety that prevents sleep.</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly selected "yes, quite a lot" and described intense panic attacks with racing heart, breathlessness, and dread, perfectly matching the highest severity option.</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly selected and described the most severe option: feeling unable to cope most of the time, overwhelmed by basic tasks, and crying with hopelessness.</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly chose "yes, most of the time" and described nightly intrusive worries preventing sleep onset plus repeated awakenings.</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly selected "yes, most of the time" and described pervasive, heavy sadness that feels overwhelming and makes daily functioning seem impossible.</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly selected "yes, most of the time" and described frequent, uncontrollable crying spells that occur "most of the time," matching the highest severity option.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 22/30 places you well above the 14-point threshold indicating probable <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. You endorse core symptoms: depressed mood most of the time, markedly diminished interest (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), fatigue, feelings of worthlessness (<quote>I'm failing her</quote>), <sym>recurrent crying</sym>, <sym>anxiety</sym>, and repeated <sym>panic attacks</sym>. Sleep is impaired by ruminative worry rather than infant demands alone. No self-harm ideation is present, but functional impairment is severe. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal psychiatrist
2. Continue daily safety check-ins with partner or friend
3. Prioritize 15-30 min rest periods when baby sleeps
4. Practice 4-7-8 breathing during <sym>panic</sym> surges
5. Accept help with household tasks to reduce overload
6. Begin gentle daily stroller walk for light and movement
7. Schedule EPDS re-screen in 1-2 weeks to track progress
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
